subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Pigmented skin disorders and seborrheic dermatitis
vignette: A 20-year-old man has had pale skin, white hair, and light irises since birth. Skin biopsy shows a normal number of melanocytes, but the melanin within them is markedly reduced. He has a history of multiple sunburns and an increased risk of skin cancer.
question: Which mechanism best explains this presentation?

options.text: Autoimmune destruction of melanocytes
A defect in neural crest cell differentiation into melanocytes
Increased melanocyte apoptosis triggered by ultraviolet light
Increased tyrosinase activity causing excessive melanin degradation
Decreased tyrosinase activity or defective tyrosine transport with normal melanocyte number

explanation_correct: Albinism is characterized by a normal number of melanocytes with decreased melanin production due to decreased tyrosinase activity or defective transport of tyrosine into melanosomes. The resulting lack of protective melanin markedly increases the risk of skin cancer. This differs from vitiligo, in which melanocytes are destroyed, and from Waardenburg syndrome, in which melanocyte development from neural crest is defective.

explanation_incorrect.A: Autoimmune destruction of melanocytes causes vitiligo, which produces irregular patches of complete depigmentation; in albinism the melanocyte number is normal.
explanation_incorrect.B: A defect in neural crest differentiation into melanocytes causes Waardenburg syndrome, with patchy depigmentation of skin, hair, and irises and possible deafness.
explanation_incorrect.C: Ultraviolet-triggered melanocyte apoptosis is not the mechanism of albinism; the melanocyte number is normal and the defect is in melanin synthesis.
explanation_incorrect.D: Albinism involves decreased, not increased, tyrosinase activity; increased activity would produce more pigment, not less.

educationalObjective: Albinism has normal melanocyte number but reduced melanin from low tyrosinase activity or defective tyrosine transport, raising skin cancer risk.

subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Pigmented skin disorders and seborrheic dermatitis
vignette: A 32-year-old woman in her third trimester develops symmetric brown patches on her cheeks and forehead. She has no scaling or inflammation, and the lesions are more noticeable because of her darker skin tone.
question: Which of the following best explains these hyperpigmented patches?

options.text: Autoimmune destruction of melanocytes
Acquired hyperpigmentation associated with pregnancy or oral contraceptive use
A congenital absence of melanocytes in the affected skin
A neural crest cell differentiation defect with associated deafness
A fungal infection of the stratum corneum

explanation_correct: Melasma (chloasma) is acquired hyperpigmentation associated with pregnancy, often called the 'mask of pregnancy,' or with oral contraceptive use. It is more common in patients with darker skin tones and presents as symmetric brown patches on sun-exposed areas of the face. Hormonal stimulation of melanocytes is the underlying driver.

explanation_incorrect.A: Autoimmune melanocyte destruction causes vitiligo, which produces depigmentation rather than hyperpigmentation.
explanation_incorrect.C: Congenital absence of melanocytes does not occur in melasma; melasma is acquired and hyperpigmented, with normal melanocyte numbers.
explanation_incorrect.D: A neural crest differentiation defect causing patchy depigmentation and deafness describes Waardenburg syndrome, not melasma.
explanation_incorrect.E: A fungal infection of the stratum corneum would produce scaling and inflammation, as in tinea, not smooth hyperpigmented patches.

educationalObjective: Melasma is acquired facial hyperpigmentation associated with pregnancy ('mask of pregnancy') or OCP use.

subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Pigmented skin disorders and seborrheic dermatitis
vignette: A 35-year-old woman has irregular patches of complete loss of skin pigment on her hands and around her eyes. The lesions have sharp borders and no scale. She also has autoimmune thyroid disease.
question: Which of the following best describes the pathogenesis of this condition?

options.text: Decreased tyrosinase activity with a normal number of melanocytes
Excessive melanin production stimulated by estrogen
A failure of neural crest cells to migrate, with congenital deafness
Autoimmune destruction of melanocytes, associated with other autoimmune disorders
Accumulation of keratinocytes with retained nuclei in the stratum corneum

explanation_correct: Vitiligo produces irregular patches of complete depigmentation caused by destruction of melanocytes, believed to be autoimmune. It is associated with other autoimmune disorders, such as autoimmune thyroid disease, as in this patient. Unlike albinism, the pigment loss is patchy and acquired rather than generalized and congenital, and unlike melasma it is depigmentation rather than hyperpigmentation.

explanation_incorrect.A: Decreased tyrosinase activity with a normal melanocyte number describes albinism, which causes generalized congenital pigment loss, not acquired patches.
explanation_incorrect.B: Excessive melanin production from hormonal stimulation describes melasma, which causes hyperpigmentation, not complete depigmentation.
explanation_incorrect.C: A neural crest differentiation defect with deafness describes Waardenburg syndrome, in which depigmentation is patchy and often congenital with iris or hair involvement.
explanation_incorrect.E: Retained nuclei in the stratum corneum describes parakeratosis, a microscopic keratinization finding, not a pigmentary disorder.

educationalObjective: Vitiligo is autoimmune melanocyte destruction causing irregular complete depigmentation and is associated with other autoimmune disease.

subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Pigmented skin disorders and seborrheic dermatitis
vignette: A neonate has a patch of white hair over the forehead, a bright blue iris on one side with a differently colored iris on the other, and pale skin patches. He fails his newborn hearing screen.
question: Which of the following best explains this combination of findings?

options.text: A defect in the differentiation of neural crest cells into melanocytes
Autoimmune destruction of mature melanocytes
A deficiency in tyrosinase activity with a normal melanocyte count
Hormonally mediated increased melanin deposition
A mutation in a desmosomal cadherin causing keratinocyte separation

explanation_correct: Waardenburg syndrome is caused by defects in the differentiation of neural crest cells into melanocytes, leading to patchy depigmentation of the skin, hair, and irises. It can be associated with sensorineural deafness because neural crest-derived cells also contribute to the inner ear. The combination of a white forelock, heterochromia iridis, and deafness is classic.

explanation_incorrect.B: Autoimmune melanocyte destruction causes vitiligo, which produces acquired irregular depigmented patches but is not associated with congenital deafness or a white forelock at birth.
explanation_incorrect.C: Tyrosinase deficiency with normal melanocyte numbers causes albinism, a generalized congenital pigment loss that does not include deafness or heterochromia.
explanation_incorrect.D: Hormonally mediated increased melanin deposition describes melasma, which causes hyperpigmentation, not the patchy depigmentation and deafness seen here.
explanation_incorrect.E: A desmosomal cadherin mutation would cause a blistering disorder such as pemphigus, not a congenital pigment and hearing defect.

educationalObjective: Waardenburg syndrome is a neural crest differentiation defect causing patchy depigmentation of skin, hair, and irises with deafness.

subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Pigmented skin disorders and seborrheic dermatitis
vignette: A 3-month-old infant develops an erythematous, well-demarcated rash on the scalp with greasy yellow scales. Similar scaling is noted around the eyes. The lesions are not painful and the infant is otherwise well.
question: Which of the following best describes this condition?

options.text: A type IV hypersensitivity reaction to a contact allergen
An autoimmune blistering disease targeting desmoglein
An erythematous, well-demarcated eruption with greasy yellow scales in areas rich in sebaceous glands, possibly associated with Malassezia
A pruritic flexural eruption with increased serum IgE and a personal history of atopy
A viral exanthem with fluid-filled vesicles in a dermatomal distribution

explanation_correct: Seborrheic dermatitis produces erythematous, well-demarcated plaques with greasy yellow scales in areas rich in sebaceous glands, such as the scalp, face, and periocular region. In infants it is known as cradle cap, matching this presentation. It is possibly associated with Malassezia species, and the sebaceous glands themselves are not inflamed even though they play a role in disease development.

explanation_incorrect.A: A type IV hypersensitivity to contact allergen describes allergic contact dermatitis, such as poison ivy or nickel, not the greasy scaling rash of seborrheic dermatitis.
explanation_incorrect.B: An autoimmune blistering disease targeting desmoglein is pemphigus vulgaris, which produces flaccid blisters and oral erosions, not a scaly erythematous eruption.
explanation_incorrect.D: A pruritic flexural eruption with elevated IgE and atopy describes atopic dermatitis (eczema), not seborrheic dermatitis.
explanation_incorrect.E: A dermatomal vesicular eruption describes herpes zoster (shingles), not the sebaceous-area greasy scaling of seborrheic dermatitis.

educationalObjective: Seborrheic dermatitis causes greasy yellow scales on sebaceous gland-rich areas (scalp, face), called cradle cap in infants and linked to Malassezia.

subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Pigmented skin disorders and seborrheic dermatitis
vignette: A 68-year-old man with Parkinson disease develops extensive, refractory scaling and erythema of the scalp and face. His clinician notes that extensive seborrheic dermatitis can be associated with certain systemic and neurologic conditions.
question: Which association and treatment pair is most appropriate for this patient?

options.text: Associated with HIV infection; treat with oral glucocorticoids alone
Associated with systemic sclerosis; treat with ACE inhibitors
Associated with pemphigus vulgaris; treat with dapsone
Associated with atopic dermatitis; treat with systemic antihistamines alone
Associated with HIV infection and Parkinson disease; treat with topical antifungals and glucocorticoids

explanation_correct: Extensive seborrheic dermatitis is associated with HIV infection and Parkinson disease, as well as with possibly pathogenic Malassezia species. Treatment is with topical antifungals and topical glucocorticoids, which address both the fungal colonization and the inflammation. The sebaceous glands are not inflamed but contribute to the lipid-rich environment that supports Malassezia growth.

explanation_incorrect.A: HIV infection is correctly associated, but oral glucocorticoids alone are not standard therapy; topical antifungals plus topical steroids are preferred, making this pair incomplete.
explanation_incorrect.B: Systemic sclerosis and ACE inhibitors relate to scleroderma renal crisis, not to seborrheic dermatitis.
explanation_incorrect.C: Pemphigus vulgaris is a separate autoimmune blistering disease treated with immunosuppression, not the appropriate association or therapy here.
explanation_incorrect.D: Atopic dermatitis is a distinct eczematous disease; antihistamines alone do not treat seborrheic dermatitis, which requires topical antifungals and glucocorticoids.

educationalObjective: Extensive seborrheic dermatitis is associated with HIV and Parkinson disease and is treated with topical antifungals plus glucocorticoids.
